etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English somtyme, som time, some tyme, sume time, sumtym, sumtyme, equivalent to some +‎ time.

definitions.definition: At an indefinite but stated time in the past or future.

quote.citation: 1995, John Frank Williams, The Quarantined Culture: Australian Reactions to Modernism, 1913–1939, page 219:
quote.text: But while there remains a considerable degree of consensus that the consequence of apparently losing the plot sometime between 1914 and 1918 was the cultural and economic malaise of the 1920s and 1930s, there are still some who look back on the interwar years less with criticism than with nostalgia.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) At an unstated past or future time; once; formerly.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: Did they not sometime cry "All hail" to me?

definitions.definition: Former, erstwhile; at some previous time.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: Therefore our sometime sister, now our queen / Th' imperial jointress to this warlike state

quote.citation: 1832, Thomas Noon Talfourd, Ion: A Tragedy, in Five Acts:
quote.text: Ion our sometime darling, whom we prized / As a stray gift, by bounteous Heaven dismiss'd
